## Dataset: Debris flow observation at Illgraben 2024: Event Data 15 June / 21 June

This dataset contains measurements from two debris flows recorded in 2024 at the Illgraben debris-flow observatory in Switzerland. The first debris flow was recorded on 15 June 2024 and the second debris flow was recorden on 21 June 2024. <br>This dataset contains the following reseach data for both:<br>a&#41; Cummulative rainfall measured at CD1 in the catchment. <br>b&#41; Radar-based flow height of debris flows measured at CD28.<br>Abstract<br>In recent years, the destructive impact of debris flows in alpine regions has become increasingly evident. Surge waves within debris flows increase peak discharge and magnify the hazard potential. Hence, understanding the dynamic complexity of debris flows is crucial to mitigate their risk. In order to capture the dynamic processes involved in the formation and interaction of surge waves, it is necessary to obtain distributed observations in the spatiotemporal domain. In this study, we present near-torrent distributed seismic measurements to monitor the Illgraben channel located in the Swiss Alps. With 33 nodal sensors, we detected and tracked surge waves along a 2-kilometer torrent section across the Illgraben fan, which allowed us to gain valuable new insights into the spatial scales relevant for surge wave formation and their long-distance propagation characteristics. We observed erosion-deposition waves that emerged out of the muddy flow tail and propagated with constant velocity along the torrent, reaching meter-scale flow heights within only 100s of meters of flow distance which significantly impact the hazard potential of debris flows. Our results provide valuable observations of surge waves from their formation to their annihilation. We can differentiate flow regimes based on their seismic signature and track them along the torrent, thus mapping the debris-flow evolution in time and space. The observations elucidate large-scale debris flow dynamics thus improving our understanding of hazard potential and the effectiveness of structural countermeasures.

[View this dataset in the data catalogue](https://opendata.swiss/de/dataset/debris-flow-observation-at-illgraben-2024-event-data-15-june-21-june)

## Load packages

This template targets tidyverse (2.x) and skimr (2.x) with R 4.1 or newer for the native `|>` pipe; package versions are not pinned. Install missing packages once with `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "skimr"))`.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

USER_AGENT <- "OpendataSwiss-StarterCode-R/1.0"
HTTP_TIMEOUT <- 30

get_dataset <- function(url, delim = NULL, drop_empty_unnamed = TRUE, ...) {
  if (grepl("^https?://", url)) {
    local_file <- tempfile()
    on.exit(unlink(local_file), add = TRUE)
    old_options <- options(timeout = HTTP_TIMEOUT)
    on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
    status <- download.file(url, local_file, method = "libcurl", mode = "wb",
                            quiet = TRUE, headers = c("User-Agent" = USER_AGENT))
    if (status != 0) stop("Resource download failed")
    url <- local_file
  }
  data <- read_delim(url, delim = delim, show_col_types = FALSE, ...)
  stop_for_problems(data)
  if (drop_empty_unnamed && nrow(data) > 0) {
    # Blank CSV headers (often from trailing separators) become "...n".
    unnamed <- grepl("^\\.\\.\\.[0-9]+$", names(data))
    empty_unnamed <- unnamed & map_lgl(data, ~ all(is.na(.x)))
    if (any(empty_unnamed)) {
      message("Removed empty unnamed columns: ", paste(names(data)[empty_unnamed], collapse = ", "))
      data <- data[, !empty_unnamed, drop = FALSE]
    }
  }
  data
}
```

Selected resource: **e0c9a720-6908-43b0-be42-44c61371954d** (CSV). This notebook loads only this resource.

For CSV, the delimiter and column types are guessed. Check the preview and metadata; set `delim`, `col_types`, `na`, or `locale` in `get_dataset(...)` when needed (for example, read identifiers with leading zeros as character columns). Parsing problems stop the import so they can be addressed.

## Missing values

```{r missing-values}
missing <- tibble(
  column = names(df),
  missing = map_int(df, ~ sum(is.na(.x))),
  missing_pct = map_dbl(df, ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100)
) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_pct))
missing

# Show up to 20 columns with missing values; percentages use all rows.
missing_plot <- missing |> filter(missing > 0) |> slice_head(n = 20)
if (nrow(missing_plot) > 0) {
  ggplot(missing_plot, aes(x = missing_pct, y = reorder(column, missing_pct))) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    labs(x = "Missing values (%)", y = NULL, title = "Missingness by column")
} else {
  message("No missing values to plot (or the dataset has no rows).")
}
```

```{r histograms}
# Plot up to four numeric columns, excluding non-finite values only from plots.
numeric_names <- names(select(df, where(is.numeric))) |> head(4)
for (column in numeric_names) {
  values <- df[[column]]
  values <- values[is.finite(values)]
  if (length(values) > 0) {
    plot <- ggplot(tibble(value = values), aes(x = value)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
      labs(title = column, x = column, y = "Count")
    print(plot)
  }
}
```

```{r category-counts}
# Top 10 values for up to three categorical columns, including missing values.

for (column in categorical_names) {

  df |> count(.data[[column]], sort = TRUE) |> head(10) |> print()
}
```
